Chapter 5. Remembering the Past, Shaping the Future.
As the sun dips below the horizon and the work of the day winds down, have you ever noticed how memories of old struggles seem to linger in the air? The stories of those who came before us—think of marches, sit-ins, hunger strikes—these aren’t just pages from a dusty history book. They’re alive. They’re part of what we carry with us, reminding us that the journey toward freedom is never really over.
Now, remembering the past isn’t about longing for the “good old days.” It’s about learning—really learning—from both the victories and the setbacks. When we look at movements like the fight for civil rights, the struggle to end apartheid, or the battle against colonialism, there’s a pattern that starts to emerge. Change is possible, absolutely. But it’s never guaranteed. It takes grit, careful planning, and, above all, the courage to keep pushing forward, even when it feels like the odds are stacked against you.
For lots of people, history is deeply personal. Maybe you’ve heard your grandparent talk about segregation, or listened to your parents share their memories of protesting. Or maybe a friend has told you what life was like under occupation. These aren’t just stories to pass the time. They’re guides—maps that can help us find our way through the challenges we’re facing right now. The wisdom from those earlier struggles becomes a source of strength, a reminder that none of us are ever truly alone.
But here’s something to pay attention to: remembering the past also means facing its pain. The history of racism, violence, or betrayal isn’t easy to sit with. It’s natural to want to turn away, to focus only on the moments of triumph. But if we’re serious about making a difference, honesty is essential. That means looking at the whole story—acknowledging the harm that’s been done and making a real commitment to do better moving forward.
Most people don’t realize just how much today is shaped by yesterday. The systems we struggle against now—prisons, policing, borders—weren’t created overnight. They’re built on foundations that go way back. Even the language we hear—terms like “law and order,” or the fear of the so-called “other”—these ideas have deep roots. Challenging them demands more than just raising our voices. It calls for a new way of thinking and the imagination to picture a different kind of future.
Shaping that future? It’s a mix of daunting and exhilarating. It means asking tough questions, like—what does real safety look like? Who gets to decide what’s possible in our world? How can today’s movements steer clear of repeating yesterday’s mistakes? And maybe most importantly, it means daring to dream. Refusing to settle for the way things are, and believing that something better is truly within reach.
